name: Yadadri Lakshmi Narasimha Temple
address: Yadagiri Hill, Yadagirigutta, Yadadri Bhuvanagiri
summary: Hilltop cave shrine of Lakshmi Narasimha near Bhuvanagiri, rebuilt in black granite and reopened in March 2022; one of Telangana's busiest pilgrim centres.
history: Tradition holds that the sage Yada, son of Rishyasringa, performed penance on this hill and was granted darshan of Narasimha, who remained here in several forms inside a cave. The cave shrine is several centuries old and was expanded over time. Between 2016 and March 2022 the Yadadri Temple Development Authority rebuilt and greatly enlarged the complex using Krishna shila black stone and lime mortar instead of cement. The town was renamed Yadadri in 2014; in November 2025 the state government restored the older name Yadagirigutta.
significance: Devotees come to seek relief from illness, troubles and evil influences, and the deity is popularly regarded as a healer. The annual Brahmotsavam in Phalguna (February–March) is the main festival, along with Narasimha Jayanti in Vaisakha (April–May). Sudarshana Narasimha Homam, Nitya Kalyanam and Satyanarayana Swamy Vratam are among the most-booked rituals. Many pilgrims stay on the hill and take part in giri pradakshina.

rules.dress_code: Traditional dress (dhoti/white lungi with uttariyam for men; saree or churidar with chunni for women) is mandatory for arjitha sevas, Nitya Kalyanam, Sudarshana Homam, Vratam and VIP darshan since June 2024; general queue is exempt
rules.queue: Free general (dharma) darshan and paid special/VIP darshan queues; weekends and holidays are crowded

name: Bhadrachalam Sita Ramachandraswamy Temple
address: Temple Road, Bhadrachalam, on the banks of the Godavari
summary: Riverside temple of Rama with Sita and Lakshmana on the Godavari, built in the 17th century by Kancherla Gopanna (Bhakta Ramadasu); famous for the Sri Rama Navami Kalyanam.
history: Legend says the sage Bhadra did penance on this hill, and Rama appeared to him as a four-armed Vaikuntha Rama with Sita and Lakshmana. In the 17th century Kancherla Gopanna, a revenue official (tahsildar) under the Qutb Shahi ruler Abul Hasan Tana Shah, built the present temple, reportedly using tax revenue. Popular tradition holds he was imprisoned at Golconda for this and released after Rama and Lakshmana miraculously repaid the money. Gopanna, known as Bhakta Ramadasu, composed many Telugu kirtanas on the deity.
significance: Bhadrachalam is regarded as one of the most important Rama shrines in South India. The Sita Rama Kalyanam on Sri Rama Navami (Chaitra, March–April) draws very large crowds, and the state government traditionally presents silk clothes and pearls (talambralu) for the wedding. Vaikuntha Ekadasi (December–January) with Teppotsavam on the Godavari is another major event. Devotees also visit Parnasala, about 35 km away, associated with the Ramayana.

rules.queue: Free general darshan plus paid special-entry darshan; Rama Navami Kalyanam and Pattabhishekam tickets need advance booking

name: Sri Raja Rajeshwara Swamy Temple, Vemulawada
address: Vemulawada, Rajanna Sircilla
summary: Major Shiva temple of North Telangana, popularly called Rajanna, known for the kode mokku bull-offering vow and the Dharmagundam holy tank.
history: The temple traces its origins to the Vemulawada Chalukyas, feudatories of the Rashtrakutas who ruled from here between about 750 and 973 CE; it is generally dated to the 9th–10th century. A local legend tells of King Raja Narendra, who was cured of leprosy after bathing in the Dharmagundam tank and then recovered a Shiva linga from its waters. The complex grew over the centuries and also contains shrines to Rajarajeshwari Devi, Sri Rama and others. A dargah within the precincts is often cited as a sign of communal harmony.
significance: Devotees bathe in the Dharmagundam, believed to have healing properties, before darshan. The best-known vow is kode mokku, in which a devotee leads a bull around the temple and hands it to the temple. Maha Shivaratri (February–March) draws the largest crowds, and Sri Rama Navami, Dasara and Bathukamma are also celebrated. The temple is often called Dakshina Kashi.

name: Gnana Saraswati Temple, Basara
address: Basar, on the banks of the Godavari, Nirmal
summary: One of the few major temples to Goddess Saraswati in India, on the Godavari at Basar; families bring children here for Aksharabhyasam, their first lesson in letters.
history: Legend says the sage Veda Vyasa stayed here after the Kurukshetra war to meditate and shaped the images of Saraswati, Lakshmi and Kali from sand taken from the Godavari, so the place was once called Vyasapuri. The temple is traditionally said to have been built by a local king around the 6th century. After damage in later invasions, a chief of Nandagiri is said to have restored the idols and renovated the temple in the 17th century.
significance: Parents bring young children for Aksharabhyasam, the ritual initiation into learning, believing the goddess grants knowledge. Vasanta Panchami (January–February) and Sharan Navaratri/Dasara (September–October) are the main festivals. Pilgrims bathe in the Godavari before darshan and also visit the Vyasa cave nearby.

rules.queue: Free general darshan; Aksharabhyasam in general and special sessions without advance booking

name: Ramappa Temple (Kakatiya Rudreshwara Temple)
address: Palampet, Venkatapur mandal, Mulugu
summary: 13th-century Kakatiya Shiva temple at Palampet, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021 and known for its sculptures and lightweight floating bricks.
history: An inscription dates the start of construction to 1213 CE, during the reign of the Kakatiya king Ganapati Deva, under his general Recherla Rudra. UNESCO notes that work is believed to have continued for about 40 years. The temple is popularly named after its chief sculptor, Ramappa. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in July 2021 as the Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple.
significance: The presiding deity is Shiva as Ramalingeswara, and the temple is still a place of worship as well as a protected monument. It is famous for its dolerite madanika (bracket) figures, carved pillars and a sandbox foundation with lightweight porous bricks in the tower that help make it earthquake resistant. Maha Shivaratri is the main festival. The nearby Ramappa Lake was built in the same period.

rules.footwear: Footwear must be removed before entering the temple
rules.entry: Protected monument; paid entry ticket reported for visitors

name: Thousand Pillar Temple, Hanumakonda
address: Hanamkonda–Warangal Road, Hanumakonda
summary: Kakatiya-era triple shrine (trikutalayam) to Shiva, Vishnu and Surya in Hanumakonda, named for its many intricately carved pillars.
history: The temple is generally credited to the Kakatiya king Rudra Deva and dated to about 1163 CE, though some sources give a later construction window. Its three shrines, to Rudreshwara (Shiva), Vishnu and Surya, are arranged in a star-shaped plan around a common mandapa. The complex was damaged during the Delhi Sultanate invasions of the 14th century. The Archaeological Survey of India dismantled and rebuilt the Kalyana Mandapam over several decades using the original sandbox foundation technique.
significance: Worship continues at the Rudreshwara shrine, and Maha Shivaratri (February–March) is the main festival. A large monolithic Nandi faces the Shiva shrine. The temple is one of the best-known Kakatiya monuments and is usually visited together with Warangal Fort and Bhadrakali Temple.

rules.footwear: Footwear must be removed before entering the shrine

name: Bhadrakali Temple, Warangal
address: Bhadrakali Temple Road, on the banks of Bhadrakali Lake, between Hanamkonda and Warangal
summary: Ancient hillside temple of Goddess Bhadrakali beside Bhadrakali Lake in Warangal, revered as the family deity of the Kakatiya kings.
history: According to an inscription and local tradition, the temple was founded around 625 CE by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II after his conquest of the Vengi region. The Kakatiya rulers later adopted Bhadrakali as their family goddess, and King Ganapati Deva is credited with building the adjoining lake. The temple declined after the fall of the Kakatiyas to the Delhi Sultanate. It was renovated in 1950 by Sri Ganesh Rao Sastri with support from local patrons including a Gujarati merchant, Maganlal.
significance: The goddess is depicted in a seated pose with eight arms and is worshipped in a fierce yet benevolent form. Devi Navaratri/Dasara (September–October) is the biggest festival, when the goddess is decorated in a different form each day, and the Shakambari festival in Ashadha (June–July) is also well known. Devotees visit especially on Tuesdays and Fridays.

name: Chilkur Balaji Temple
address: Chilkur village, Moinabad mandal, Rangareddy (near Osman Sagar)
summary: Old Venkateswara temple on the outskirts of Hyderabad, popularly called Visa Balaji; it accepts no money offerings and has no VIP or paid darshan.
history: Tradition says the temple dates from the time of Akkanna and Madanna, the 17th-century Golconda ministers who were uncles of Bhakta Ramadasu. A local legend tells of a devotee who could no longer travel to Tirupati and was told in a dream that the Lord was present at Chilkur, where an image was then found. The temple is one of the few in Telangana that remained outside the control of the state endowments department and is run by a hereditary family of archakas. From the 1990s it became popular with students and professionals seeking visas to study or work abroad.
significance: Devotees make a wish while walking 11 pradakshinas (circumambulations) and return to walk 108 pradakshinas once it is fulfilled. The temple has no hundi, accepts no cash offerings and does not sell special-entry or VIP darshan tickets, so everyone uses the same queue. Brahmotsavam and Vaikuntha Ekadasi are the main festivals. Weekends and holidays are very crowded.

rules.entry: Open to all; no VIP, special or paid darshan; no hundi or money offerings accepted
rules.queue: Single free queue for everyone; weekday mornings are least crowded

pujas.name: Pradakshina vow
pujas.description: Wish-making with 11 pradakshinas, and 108 pradakshinas in thanksgiving once the wish is fulfilled.

name: Birla Mandir, Hyderabad
address: Hill Fort Road, Naubat Pahad, Khairatabad, Hyderabad
summary: White-marble Venkateswara temple built by the Birla family in 1976 on Naubat Pahad hill, overlooking Hussain Sagar in central Hyderabad.
history: The temple was built by the Birla Foundation of the Birla family and completed in 1976 on Naubat Pahad (also called Kala Pahad), a 280-foot hillock. It was constructed with about 2,000 tonnes of white Rajasthani marble. The main idol of Venkateswara is about 11 feet tall, with separate shrines for Padmavati and Andal. The temple was consecrated by Swami Ranganathananda of the Ramakrishna Mission.
significance: The temple is open to all and is a popular stop for both pilgrims and tourists, especially in the evening when it is lit up and offers views over the city and Hussain Sagar. Vaikuntha Ekadasi and Sri Rama Navami are among the festivals celebrated. Unusually, there are no bells in the temple, keeping it quiet for meditation.
architecture_style: Blend of South Indian (Dravidian), Rajasthani and Utkala styles

rules.mobile: Mobile phones not allowed inside the temple complex; deposit at the counter
rules.footwear: Footwear deposited before climbing to the shrine

name: Jogulamba Temple, Alampur
address: Alampur, at the confluence of the Tungabhadra and Krishna, Jogulamba Gadwal
summary: Temple of Goddess Jogulamba at Alampur, the fifth of the 18 Ashtadasa Shakti Peethas, beside the Navabrahma group of early Chalukyan Shiva temples.
history: Tradition holds that Sati's upper jaw (teeth) fell at Alampur, making it one of the 18 Maha Shakti Peethas. The surrounding Navabrahma temples, dedicated to Shiva as Balabrahmeswara and others, were built by the Badami Chalukyas in the 7th–8th centuries. The original Jogulamba shrine was destroyed in the 14th century during the Bahmani period, and the deity was kept for centuries in the Balabrahmeswara temple. A new temple was built on the original site in 2005 and the goddess was reinstalled there.
significance: Devotees worship Jogulamba as a powerful form of Shakti and visit Balabrahmeswara Swamy in the same complex. Navaratri/Dasara (September–October) and Maha Shivaratri are the main festivals. Alampur is also called the western gateway to Srisailam. The site lies near the confluence of the Tungabhadra and Krishna rivers.
architecture_style: Badami Chalukya (Navabrahma temples); main shrine rebuilt 2005

name: Sammakka Saralamma Temple, Medaram
address: Medaram, Tadvai mandal, Mulugu
summary: Forest shrine of the tribal goddesses Sammakka and Saralamma at Medaram, site of the biennial Medaram Jatara, one of the largest tribal gatherings in India.
history: Koya oral tradition says that in the 13th century the Kakatiya king Prataparudra imposed taxes on the Koya chief Pagididda Raju, which he could not pay during a drought. In the battle that followed, Pagididda Raju, his daughter Saralamma and others were killed, and Sammakka, after fighting bravely, disappeared into the forest near Chilakalagutta, where only a vermilion casket was found. The Koya people deified mother and daughter and began a festival in their honour every two years. The goddesses are represented by sacred poles and vermilion on raised platforms (gaddelu) rather than by idols.
significance: The Medaram Jatara is held every two years for four days in Magha (January–February). On the first day Saralamma is brought from Kannepalli, and on the second Sammakka is brought from Chilakalagutta to the gaddelu, with rituals performed by Koya priests. Pilgrims bathe in the Jampanna Vagu stream and offer jaggery, called bangaram (gold), equal to their own weight. Crowds are estimated at over a crore people, and it is often called the Kumbh Mela of the tribals.

pujas.name: Bangaram offering
pujas.description: Offering of jaggery equal to one's body weight to the goddesses.

name: Komuravelli Mallikarjuna Swamy Temple
address: Komuravelli hill, Komuravelli mandal, Siddipet
summary: Hill-cave shrine of Mallanna (Mallikarjuna Swamy, a form of Shiva) with his consorts Golla Ketamma and Medalamma, a major folk pilgrimage centre of Telangana.
history: The temple stands in a cave on a small hill at Komuravelli. According to local tradition, a devotee named Komaranna of the Yadava (Golla) community installed the deity on the hill. The main image is moulded from clay and is believed to be about 500 years old. Mallanna's story, including his marriage to Medalamma, is not written down but is preserved in the Oggu Katha ballad tradition sung by Oggu pujaris.
significance: The deity is especially revered by pastoral and farming communities, who come to fulfil vows and offer bonam (cooked rice offerings). The jatara season runs from Makara Sankranti (January) to Ugadi (March–April) and includes Brahmotsavam, Pedda Patnam on Maha Shivaratri, and Agni Gundalu (fire-walking) on the Sunday before Ugadi. Oggu pujaris draw large coloured-powder designs called patnam as offerings. Sundays during the jatara see the biggest crowds.

name: Kondagattu Anjaneya Swamy Temple
address: Kondagattu hill, near Muthyampet, Mallial mandal, Jagtial
summary: Hilltop Hanuman temple near Jagtial, the main centre of Hanuman Deeksha in Telangana, drawing lakhs of devotees around Hanuman Jayanti.
history: Local legend says that about 300 years ago a cowherd named Singam Sanjeevudu, searching for a lost cow, fell asleep on the hill and was told by Anjaneya in a dream where to find it; on waking he found the idol of Anjaneya there. The present temple is credited to Krishna Rao Deshmukh, a local landlord, though sources differ on when he rebuilt it. The idol is notable for showing Anjaneya with two faces, one of them Narasimha.
significance: Many devotees take the 41-day Hanuman Deeksha and walk long distances to Kondagattu to complete it, carrying irumudi up the hill. Hanuman Jayanti (Chinna and Pedda Jayanti in Chaitra and Vaisakha) is the main festival and draws several lakh pilgrims. The temple is also popular with couples praying for children, and Tuesdays and Saturdays are busy.

name: Kaleshwara Mukteswara Swamy Temple, Kaleshwaram
address: Kaleshwaram, Mahadevpur mandal, Jayashankar Bhupalpally
summary: Ancient Shiva temple at the Triveni Sangamam of the Godavari, Pranahita and the hidden Saraswati, unusual for its two lingas on a single pedestal.
history: The temple enshrines two lingas on one pedestal: Mukteswara, representing Shiva, and Kaleshwara, representing Yama. A popular legend says Yama, finding that people freed of sins at Mukteswara were bypassing his realm, did penance here and Shiva allowed him a linga beside his own. Kaleshwaram is counted as one of the three Trilinga kshetras, with Srisailam and Draksharamam, that are said to give Telangana its name. In 2026 a Rs 198-crore redevelopment of the temple began, and daily rituals were shifted to a balalayam at the nearby Adi Mukteswara Swamy temple.
significance: Pilgrims bathe at the confluence (Triveni Sangamam) before worshipping both lingas, believing it frees them from sins and grants moksha. Maha Shivaratri and Kartika masam (October–November) are the main festivals. The temple hosts the Pranahita and Saraswati Pushkaralu, held once every 12 years. A notable feature is a hole in the Mukteswara linga said never to fill with water.

name: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Dharmapuri
address: Dharmapuri, on the banks of the Godavari, Jagtial
summary: Narasimha temple at Dharmapuri on the Godavari, where the river flows south (Dakshina Vahini); known for its Yama Dharmaraja shrine at the entrance.
history: Dharmapuri is mentioned in inscriptions from about the 10th century, and the temple is dated to the Chalukya period, with later expansion under the Kakatiyas, roughly between the 11th and 13th centuries. Legend links the town's name to King Dharmavarma, who is said to have done penance here. The complex has shrines to Ugra (fierce) and Yoga/Saumya (peaceful) forms of Narasimha, along with a Venkateswara shrine, a Shiva temple and a shrine of Yama.
significance: Pilgrims bathe in the Godavari, which flows north to south here and is considered especially holy. Devotees traditionally pray first to Yama Dharmaraja at the entrance to be spared an untimely death, then to Anjaneya, before the main deity. The 13-day Brahmotsavam from Phalguna Shuddha Ekadasi (usually March) includes the Kalyanam and a chariot procession. Godavari Pushkaralu is also celebrated here.

name: Keesaragutta Sri Ramalingeswara Swamy Temple
address: Keesaragutta hill, Keesara mandal, Medchal-Malkajgiri
summary: Hillock Shiva temple about 30 km from Hyderabad, where tradition says Rama installed a linga; the hill is strewn with lingas said to have been brought by Hanuman.
history: Legend says Rama wished to install a Shiva linga here to atone for killing Ravana and sent Hanuman to Varanasi to fetch one. When Hanuman was late for the auspicious hour, Shiva appeared and gave a linga himself, which Rama installed as Ramalingeswara. Hanuman returned with 101 lingas and, disappointed, scattered them across the hill; Rama then ordained that Hanuman would be worshipped first, and the hill came to be called Kesarigiri, later Keesaragutta. Archaeological finds on the hill include rock-cut caves with an early Telugu inscription of about the 5th century CE and remains associated with the Vishnukundina period.
significance: Maha Shivaratri (February–March) is the biggest festival and draws several lakh devotees, and Kartika masam (October–November) is also busy. Devotees worship the many lingas scattered on the hill. It is one of the most popular Shiva temples near Hyderabad.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad, about 60 km

name: Ujjaini Mahankali Temple, Secunderabad
address: General Bazaar, M.G. Road, Secunderabad
summary: Temple of Goddess Mahankali in Secunderabad founded in 1815 by a soldier returning from Ujjain; centre of the Lashkar Bonalu festival.
history: In 1813 a cholera epidemic struck Hyderabad and Secunderabad. Suriti Appaiah, a doli bearer in a military battalion posted to Ujjain, prayed at the Mahakali temple there and vowed to install the goddess in Secunderabad if the epidemic ended. On returning, he and his associates installed a wooden image of Mahankali in July 1815. A stone image of Manikyalamma was found during construction and installed beside her, and a stone image of Mahankali replaced the wooden one in 1964. The temple is managed by the Telangana Endowments Department, with the founder's family retaining a hereditary role.
significance: The temple is the focus of Lashkar (Secunderabad) Bonalu in the month of Ashadha (July–August), when lakhs of women carry bonam pots of cooked rice to the goddess. The day after Bonalu, a female oracle delivers Rangam, a prophecy for the coming year, followed by the Ghatam procession. Devotees pray to the goddess for protection from disease and misfortune.

pujas.name: Bonam offering
pujas.description: Offering of cooked rice with jaggery in a decorated pot to the goddess.

name: Balkampet Yellamma Temple
address: Balkampet, near S.R. Nagar / Ameerpet, Hyderabad
summary: Hyderabad temple of Goddess Yellamma, whose self-manifested image lies about 10 feet below ground in spring water; famous for its Ashadha Kalyanotsavam.
history: Tradition holds that the image of the goddess was found by people digging a well, carved on a rock deep below ground level; it is treated as a self-manifested (swayambhu) image and the goddess is also called Jala Durga. The shrine is commonly dated to around the 15th century, and the present temple building is usually dated to 1919. The temple is administered by the Telangana Endowments Department.
significance: Water from the spring at the deity's feet is taken home as tirtham and is believed to have healing properties. The Yellamma Kalyanotsavam, held on the first Tuesday of Ashadha (June–July), and the Bonalu that follow draw very large crowds and are attended by state ministers. Sundays and Tuesdays are busy throughout the year.

pujas.name: Yellamma Kalyanotsavam
pujas.description: Annual celestial wedding of the goddess.

nearest.bus: Ameerpet / S.R. Nagar, about 1 km (Metro: Ameerpet)

name: Sri Simhavahini Mahankali Temple, Lal Darwaza
address: Lal Darwaza, Old City, Hyderabad
summary: Old City shrine of Goddess Mahankali seated on a lion, best known as the venue where Hyderabad's Ashada Bonalu season comes to its close.
history: The goddess is worshipped here as Simhavahini, the lion-riding form of Mahankali. Accounts link the shrine's rise to the great Musi flood of September 1908: according to temple tradition, the sixth Nizam, Mir Mahbub Ali Khan, on the advice of his prime minister Maharaja Kishen Pershad, offered pearls in a silver vessel to the river and to the goddess, after which the waters receded. One account says the Nizam had donated land for the temple in 1905. These details rest on oral tradition and temple committee accounts rather than contemporary records; the Lal Darwaza Bonalu has been held for well over a century (the 2026 festival was described as the 118th).
significance: Lal Darwaza hosts the last and one of the largest stages of the Ashada Bonalu festival (July-August), after Golconda and Secunderabad Ujjaini Mahankali. Women carry decorated pots of cooked rice (bonam) as offerings, followed the next day by the Rangam oracle and the Ghatam procession to the Musi near Afzalgunj. The temple is also visited through the year by devotees seeking protection from illness and misfortune.

rules.footwear: Remove footwear before entering the shrine
rules.queue: Very heavy crowds and long queues on Bonalu days; police-managed queue lines are set up

name: Sri Ranganatha Swamy Temple, Jiyaguda
address: Jiyaguda, on the banks of the Musi River, Hyderabad
summary: Roughly 400-year-old Vaishnava temple to Lord Ranganatha on the Musi riverbank in Jiyaguda, one of the oldest Vishnu shrines in Hyderabad.
history: The temple is about four centuries old and is credited to the Nanganur (Vanamamalai) Prathama Peetham of Sri Vaishnavas. Local tradition holds that Kalyana Vanamamalai Ramanuja Jeeyar, head of the peetham, stayed here, giving the locality the name Jeeyarguda, later Jiyaguda. In Qutb Shahi times the surrounding area was the trading settlement of Karwan. Worship originally followed the Thenkalai tradition and later the Vanamamalai sampradayam. The temple is now administered by the Telangana Endowments Department.
significance: Vaikuntha Ekadasi (December-January) is the main festival, when large crowds come for darshan through the northern Vaikuntha Dwaram. The temple also observes Brahmotsavams and Sri Vaishnava festivals of Ranganatha. Its riverside setting and old complex make it a heritage landmark of the old city.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad, about 25 km

name: Sri Ashtalakshmi Temple, Vasavi Colony
address: Vasavi Colony, Kothapet (between Dilsukhnagar and LB Nagar), Hyderabad
summary: Modern temple in Vasavi Colony dedicated to the eight forms of Goddess Lakshmi, consecrated in 1996 and modelled on the Ashtalakshmi temple in Chennai.
history: The foundation stone was laid on 23 February 1991 and construction took more than five years. The temple was consecrated in April 1996 under the guidance of the Kanchi Kamakoti Peetham, with Sri Jayendra Saraswathi performing the ceremony. Its plan was adapted, with modifications, from the Ashtalakshmi temple at Besant Nagar, Chennai. It was built by devotees in the Vasavi Colony housing layout near the Hyderabad-Vijayawada highway.
significance: Devotees worship Lakshmi in her eight aspects, including Adi, Dhanya, Dhairya, Gaja, Santana, Vijaya, Vidya and Dhana Lakshmi, for prosperity and family welfare. Fridays are especially busy, and the temple holds Navaratri (September-October), Sravana masam celebrations including Varalakshmi Vratam (July-August) and an annual Brahmotsavam. It closes during solar and lunar eclipses.

rules.queue: Crowded on Fridays and during Navaratri and Sravana masam

pujas.name: Abhishekam
pujas.description: Ritual bathing of the deity performed weekly.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad, about 30 km
nearest.bus: Kothapet / Dilsukhnagar bus stops, about 1-2 km

name: Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple (TTD), Himayatnagar
address: TTD Balaji Bhavan, Himayatnagar, Hyderabad
summary: Temple of Lord Venkateswara run by Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams at its Balaji Bhavan in Himayatnagar, central Hyderabad.
history: Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD) maintains the Balaji Bhavan in Himayatnagar, which serves as a temple and information centre for Tirumala pilgrims in Hyderabad. The temple follows Tirumala worship traditions. Its annual Brahmotsavams reached their 20th edition in June 2026, which suggests the present temple dates from the mid-2000s.
significance: The temple gives Hyderabad devotees darshan of Venkateswara in the Tirumala tradition without travelling to Tirupati. Annual Brahmotsavams (May-June) feature morning and evening vahana sevas, and on Vaikuntha Ekadasi the temple opens from about 2 a.m. for Uttara Dwara darshan.

rules.dress_code: Traditional dress is customary in TTD temples
rules.queue: Heavy crowds on Vaikuntha Ekadasi and Saturdays

pujas.description: Processions of the utsava deity on different vahanams during the annual Brahmotsavams.

name: Statue of Equality and 108 Divya Desam Temples, Muchintal
address: Sri Ramanagaram, Muchintal, Shamshabad, Hyderabad
summary: A 216-ft seated statue of Sri Ramanujacharya ringed by stone replicas of the 108 Divya Desam shrines, part of Chinna Jeeyar Swamy's ashram complex near Shamshabad.
history: The complex was conceived by Tridandi Chinna Jeeyar Swamy to mark the 1,000th birth anniversary of the 11th-century philosopher Ramanujacharya. The 216-ft panchaloha statue was unveiled by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in February 2022 during the Sahasrabdi celebrations. A 120-kg gold idol of Ramanuja is installed in the sanctum within the Bhadra Vedi base. Around the statue, 108 shrines built in black stone reproduce the 108 Divya Desams praised by the Alvars, linked by a covered corridor.
significance: The site lets devotees visit representations of all 108 Divya Desams of Vishnu in one place, and it honours Ramanuja's teaching that all people are equal before God. The annual Samatha Kumbh celebrations around the anniversary (February) draw large crowds. A musical laser show on the statue is held in the evenings.

rules.dress_code: Shoulders and knees must be covered; traditional dress preferred
rules.mobile: Mobile phones not allowed; deposit at cloakroom
rules.footwear: Remove footwear before entering the shrine area
rules.entry: Entry by pass, available at walk-in counters or online; food, bags, pets, tobacco and sharp objects are not allowed

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad, about 15 km

name: Sri Seetha Ramachandra Swamy Temple, Ammapalli
address: Ammapalli, Narkhuda village, Shamshabad mandal
summary: Old temple of Sita, Rama and Lakshmana near Shamshabad with a large stepwell, long a film location and now a popular wedding venue.
history: Local legend says Rama rested here on his way to the Dandakaranya forest. There are no inscriptions on site, and accounts differ on its age: it is variously attributed to the Chalukyas between the 7th and 13th centuries, most often to the 12th-13th century. According to the priests, the sanctum and mandapa are the oldest parts, while the gopuram and the pillared corridors around the stepwell were added in the 17th century. The complex covers about nine acres.
significance: The sanctum images of Sita, Rama and Lakshmana are carved from a single stone, and unusually there is no Hanuman beside them, as he had not yet joined Rama during the exile. Sri Rama Navami (March-April) is the main festival, when Sri Rama Kalyanam draws tens of thousands of devotees. Hundreds of Telugu films were shot here until filming was stopped, and the temple is now sought after for weddings.

rules.photography: Film shooting is no longer permitted
rules.queue: Large crowds on Sri Rama Navami

pujas.name: Sri Rama Kalyanam
pujas.description: Celestial wedding of Sita and Rama performed on Sri Rama Navami.

name: Sri Ganesh Temple, Secunderabad
address: Station Road, beside Secunderabad Railway Station, Secunderabad
summary: About 200-year-old Ganesha temple beside Secunderabad railway station, built around an idol said to have been found in a well in 1824.
history: According to temple tradition, sepoys of the Madras Regiment found the Ganesha idol in 1824 while digging a well in the cantonment. A shrine was built for the idol, which became the presiding deity, and the temple grew over the following two centuries. The temple states that the idol's installation was performed under the Kanchi Kamakoti Peetham. The complex now includes several sub-shrines.
significance: It is one of the best-known Ganesha temples in the twin cities and is busy on Tuesdays and Sankashti Chaturthi. Vinayaka Chavithi (August-September) is the main festival. Devotees perform daily homams and Ganapathi Kalyanam, and many travellers stop here before journeys from the adjacent station.

name: Sri Kurumurthy Venkateswara Swamy Temple, Ammapur
address: Kurumurthy hills, Ammapur, Chinna Chintakunta mandal
summary: Hill shrine of Lord Venkateswara (Kurumurthy Swamy) near Ammapur, host of the largest annual jatara in the Mahabubnagar region.
history: Legend holds that Goddess Lakshmi asked Lord Srinivasa to manifest on these hills, and the name Kurumurthy is linked to the Telugu for 'place where the Lord resides'. The image is said to have stayed in a hill cave for centuries until a local chieftain, Mukkara Chandra Reddy, built a temple on the hill and enshrined it. Sources date the temple to about 1350 CE.
significance: The annual Kurumurthy jatara, held over about 19 days in the Karthika season (October-November), is the biggest fair in the district. A highlight is the offering of a new pair of leather sandals (uddalu), made by residents of nearby Vaddeman village who fast while making them, which are carried in procession and placed in the Uddala mandapam. Devotees fulfil vows such as head-shaving and offerings to the deity.

rules.footwear: Remove footwear before climbing to the shrine
rules.queue: Very large crowds during the jatara

pujas.name: Uddala procession (sandal offering)
pujas.description: Procession presenting new handmade sandals to the deity.

name: Manyamkonda Sri Lakshmi Venkateswara Swamy Temple
address: Manyamkonda hill, near Devarakadra, on the Mahabubnagar-Raichur road (NH 167)
summary: Cave shrine of Lord Venkateswara atop the Manyamkonda hills near Mahabubnagar, popularly called the Tirupati of Palamuru.
history: The hill was once known as Munulakonda because sages such as Narasimha Yogi, Kasirayalu, Veerappaiah and Ettepu Ramayogi are believed to have meditated here; the name later became Manyamkonda. The devotional singer Hanumadasu (Narayana Konda Hanumadas) is associated with the place. The deity is enshrined in a natural cave on top of the hills, about 16-22 km from Mahabubnagar town.
significance: Known as Palamoor Tirupathi, the temple is a major Venkateswara pilgrimage for the Mahabubnagar region and is regarded as a Harihara kshetra. The main annual festival falls on Magha Purnima (February), drawing large numbers of pilgrims. Saturdays in Sravana and Karthika months are also busy.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad, about 110 km

name: Sri Satyanarayana Swamy Temple, Gudem
address: Gudem Gutta (Ratnagiri hill), Gudem village, Dandepalli mandal
summary: Hilltop temple of Lord Satyanarayana above the Godavari at Gudem, often called the Annavaram of Telangana.
history: According to local tradition, in 1964 Lord Satyanarayana appeared in a dream to a Gudem resident, Govardhana Perumandla Swamy, revealing that he was on the Ratnapu hill; idols were then found on the hill. With help from villagers, a temple was built on the hilltop. The hill was earlier known as Ratnadri.
significance: Devotees perform the Satyanarayana Swamy Vratam here, as at Annavaram, for family welfare and fulfilment of vows. Pilgrim numbers peak in Karthika masam (October-November), when devotees bathe in the Godavari before worship. A seven-day annual Brahmotsavam is also held.

pujas.name: Satyanarayana Swamy Vratam
pujas.description: Vratam to Lord Satyanarayana performed by devotees with the help of temple priests.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad, about 280 km

name: Sri Koteswara Siddeswara Swamy Temple, Kotilingala
address: Kotilingala village, Velgatoor mandal, on the Godavari
summary: Shiva temple on the Godavari at Kotilingala, beside an early historic fortified site linked to the pre-Satavahana and early Satavahana period.
history: Kotilingala is an important archaeological site: excavations revealed a mud fort about 1 km long and punch-marked coins of local rulers Gobhada and Samagopa from around the 2nd-3rd century BCE, and coins bearing the name Simuka, leading some to call it an early Satavahana capital (a view scholars debate). The name Koteshwara is linked to the Shiva shrine standing inside this kota or fort. Some local sources attribute the temple to the Satavahanas, but this dating is not confirmed. The present shrine is the focus of worship on the riverbank.
significance: Devotees bathe in the Godavari at the riverside ghat before worshipping Koteswara Siddeswara Swamy. The site is a major bathing point during Godavari Pushkaralu (next due in 2027, with new ghats planned), and is also busy in Karthika masam and on Maha Shivaratri. Its archaeological remains add heritage interest to the pilgrimage.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad, about 250 km

name: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Bejjanki
address: Rocky hillock, Bejjanki village
summary: Kakatiya-era hilltop temple of Lakshmi Narasimha at Bejjanki, the surviving shrine among several ruined medieval temples around the village.
history: Bejjanki is a historic village surrounded by ruins of several Kakatiya-period temples. The Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy temple, built on top of a rocky hillock, is the one that survived in use. Much of its sculpture was deliberately damaged in the past, but enough of the carving and architecture remains to be of interest to scholars. The village lies about 40 km southwest of Karimnagar.
significance: The temple is a local centre of Narasimha worship for the Siddipet-Karimnagar area. Festivals noted include Vasantha Panchami (January-February), Navaratri (September-October) and Shani Trayodashi. Free meals (annadanam) for devotees are reported at the temple premises.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad, about 150 km

name: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy Temple, Nampally Gutta
address: Nampally Gutta, on the Vemulawada-Karimnagar road, near Vemulawada
summary: Hillock shrine of Lakshmi Narasimha near Vemulawada, known for its giant serpent-shaped tunnel that leads devotees through scenes of the Prahlada story.
history: The temple stands on a small hillock beside the Vemulawada-Karimnagar road. The main image of Narasimha is carved from the rock around which the shrine was built. A later addition is a large structure in the form of a serpent: devotees enter through its body, a long winding tunnel lined with figures telling the story of Prahlada and Hiranyakashipu, ending at an image of Narasimha slaying the demon. Telangana Tourism notes the shrine does not appear ancient; no founding date is published.
significance: Pilgrims visiting the Raja Rajeshwara temple at Vemulawada commonly stop here. The serpent tunnel and the image of Narasimha emerging from a pillar at the entrance make it popular with families. Narasimha Jayanti (April-May) and Saturdays draw more devotees.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad, about 180 km

name: Sri Kondapochamma Temple, Siddipet
address: Near Kondapochamma Sagar reservoir, Siddipet district
summary: Folk shrine of Goddess Kondapochamma, guardian deity of the area, closely linked to the Komuravelli Mallanna pilgrimage and the reservoir named Kondapochamma Sagar.
history: Kondapochamma is a village guardian goddess worshipped in the Telangana folk tradition. Local belief, transmitted orally rather than in scripture, holds that she is the sister of Mallanna, the deity of Komuravelli. The Kaleshwaram project's Kondapochamma Sagar reservoir lies near the shrine. No founding date is recorded.
significance: Many pilgrims to the Komuravelli Mallanna jatara (Sankranti to Ugadi, January-March) also visit Kondapochamma. Bonalu and Navaratri are the main festivals, when devotees offer bonam pots and fulfil vows for family welfare.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad

name: Sri Chennakesava Swamy Temple, Gangapuram
address: Gangapuram village, Jadcherla mandal, about 5 km from Jadcherla towards Kalwakurthy
summary: Medieval Chalukya-period temple of Chenna Kesava (Vishnu) with Lakshmi at Gangapuram near Jadcherla, known for its Ratha Saptami festival.
history: Local sources date the temple to about 1042 CE and credit the Kalyani Chalukya king Trailokyamalla Someshvara I, when the place was called Kesavapuram; other accounts describe it as a 12th-century temple, and the dating is not confirmed by a published inscription. Earlier names recorded for the village include Mayapuram, Matsyapuram and Duritapuram. The surrounding area also shows traces of Jaina, Kalamukha and Shaiva activity. The temple is said to be mentioned in the Skanda Purana.
significance: The main festival is held on Ratha Saptami (January-February), drawing large numbers of people from the region; Brahmotsavam and Kalyanotsavam are also celebrated. Besides Chenna Kesava and Lakshmi, the temple has shrines of Anjaneya and a four-armed Ganapathi. Its outer hall has 20 old carved pillars, 12 of them facing the sanctum.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad, about 75 km

name: Ghanpur Group of Temples (Kota Gullu), Ghanpur
address: Ghanpur village, Ghanpur (Mulugu) mandal, about 9 km north-west of Ramappa
summary: Walled Kakatiya-era complex of about 22 stone temples at Ghanpur near Ramappa, centred on a Shiva temple known as Ganapeswaralayam.
history: The temples were built in the reign of the Kakatiya king Ganapatideva (c. 1199-1262). A slab inscription of about 1234-35 CE records Ganapathi Reddy installing the Ganapeswara shrine and granting land. The name Kota Gullu means 'fort temples', from the stone enclosure around the group. The complex was badly damaged, either by invasions between the 14th and 16th centuries or by a later earthquake, and is now protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.
significance: The main Shiva temple, with fine sculpture and bracket figures in the style of nearby Ramappa, is the highlight and is still visited by devotees, especially on Maha Shivaratri (February-March). The site is of strong interest for Kakatiya art and architecture and is often combined with a visit to the Ramappa temple.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad, about 230 km

name: Sri Erakeswara Swamy Temple, Pillalamarri
address: Pillalamarri village, about 6-8 km north-west of Suryapet
summary: Early 13th-century Kakatiya-style Shiva temple at Pillalamarri, part of a group of Recherla-built temples near Suryapet.
history: The Erakeswara temple was built around 1208 CE by the Recherla chiefs, feudatories of the Kakatiyas; one account credits Erakasani, wife of Beti Reddi of the Recherla family, after whom the god is named. It stands in a village with several contemporary temples, including the Nameswara temple built by Nami Reddy around 1202 CE, the Trikuteswara temple and a Chennakesava temple. Inscriptions at the site mention the Kakatiya rulers Rudradeva and Ganapatideva.
significance: The temple is noted for its Kakatiya sculpture, carved pillars and ceiling panels, and is still a place of local Shiva worship, with Maha Shivaratri (February-March) the main occasion. It is one of the important Kakatiya heritage sites of the Nalgonda-Suryapet region.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad, about 150 km

name: Sri Veerabhadra Swamy Temple, Kothakonda
address: Kothakonda village, Bheemadevarapalli mandal
summary: Temple of Veerabhadra Swamy at the foot of a fortified hill in Kothakonda, famous for its large three-day Sankranti jatara.
history: The temple stands at the foot of a rocky hill whose top bears the ruins of a large fort with gateways in a style resembling Kakatiya work. Veerabhadra, a fierce form of Shiva, is enshrined flanked by Kethamma and Medalamma. No documented founding date is published.
significance: The Kothakonda jatara, also called the Veerabhadra Swamy Brahmotsavam, is held for three days around Makara Sankranti in January and draws thousands of pilgrims from across Telangana. Maha Shivaratri and Devi Navaratri are also celebrated. Devotees fulfil vows and take part in the Bhadrakali-Veerabhadra kalyanam.

rules.queue: Large crowds during the January jatara

pujas.name: Veerabhadra Swamy Kalyanam
pujas.description: Celestial wedding of Veerabhadra and Bhadrakali performed during the annual festivals.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad, about 180 km

name: Ratnalayam Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple, Shamirpet
address: Near Shamirpet Lake, Shamirpet, Hyderabad
summary: White-stone Dravidian temple of Lord Venkateswara near Shamirpet Lake on Hyderabad's northern edge, consecrated in 2003.
history: The temple was built by T. R. Venkatesh and T. Rama Devi in memory of his father, to give devotees who could not travel to Tirumala a place to worship Venkateswara. Bhoomi puja was held in April 2001 and the temple was consecrated in February 2003. The architect was M. Shankar, and the idols were carved by Ganapathi Sthapathi of Kanchipuram.
significance: The temple follows Tirumala-style worship of Venkateswara and is popular with Hyderabad families for darshan, tonsuring and weddings. The complex includes a Kalyana Katta, discourse hall, goshala, gardens and fountains, and sits close to Shamirpet Lake.

nearest.airport: Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Shamshabad, about 60 km
